result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.common_neighbors()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the number of common neighbors for node pairs. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L8618-L8696){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.common_neighbors(ebunch=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Common neighbors](/assets/graphs/algo-common-neighbors.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two focal nodes A and B, unconnected to each other, with two common neighbors between them. The focal pair, the shared neighbors, and the edges linking them are all shown in the accent color; each focal node's unique neighbor is drawn in default styling." width="100%"} For each pair of nodes `(u, v)`, counts how many nodes are neighbors of both `u` and `v`. Common neighbors is a simple but effective link prediction measure. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ebunch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[tuple[Union[int, str], Union[int, str]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : List of node pairs to compute predictions for. Each pair can use node IDs (integers) or labels (strings). If `None`, computes for all pairs of nodes that are not already connected. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of `(u, v, count)` tuples where count is the number of common neighbors. Results are returned with node IDs. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For each candidate pair $(u, v)$, the score is simply $|N(u) \cap N(v)|$, computed in $O(k)$ per pair on undirected simple graphs (where $k$ is the average degree). Despite its crudeness, the metric remains a competitive baseline for link prediction in social networks with high clustering: the more mutual friends two people share, the more likely they are to befriend each other. It ignores degree entirely, so hubs dominate; the Jaccard, Adamic-Adar, and resource-allocation variants below correct for that in different ways. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Without an explicit `ebunch=`, every currently-unconnected pair is scored -- Alice and Carol share Bob as a mutual friend, so that pair gets a nonzero score: ::: {#9728e17f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) for name in ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave"]: graph.add_node(label=name) # Alice and Carol share Bob as a friend graph.add_edge(source="Alice", target="Bob") graph.add_edge(source="Carol", target="Bob") graph.add_edge(source="Carol", target="Dave") graph.common_neighbors() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(3, 1, 1), (1, 4, 0), (4, 2, 1)] ``` ::: ::: Passing `ebunch=` restricts the computation to specific pairs -- useful when only a handful of candidate links need scoring: ::: {#348faf73 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) for name in ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave"]: graph.add_node(label=name) graph.add_edge(source="Alice", target="Bob") graph.add_edge(source="Carol", target="Bob") graph.common_neighbors([("Alice", "Carol"), ("Alice", "Dave")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [(1, 3, 1), (1, 4, 0)] ``` ::: :::
